correspondence.finding: The northern piece begins in the headwater setting east of Passo Fundo, continues south and southwest through the Ernestina water-body setting, then approaches the Espumoso sector. The Alto Jacuí sheet shows this continuous eastern headwater-to-main-river corridor, distinct from the Jacuí-Mirim and Colorado approaches farther west. The SGB report independently locates the Jacuí source in eastern Passo Fundo; the model endpoint is not asserted to be that surveyed or officially fixed source.

The next piece continues west and southwest below Espumoso and Alto Alegre into the large branching water-body corridor. The following long piece proceeds south through the Salto do Jacuí setting, bends past the Ivaí approach, and continues through the Pinhal Grande–Ibarama sector toward Dona Francisca. Repeated Rio Jacuí labels, water-body outlines and the river's distinctive bends on the Alto and Baixo sheets correspond to this actual course. Named reservoir settings are not converted into river aliases.

From the Dona Francisca sector, the lower piece continues south past Agudo and the Restinga Seca approach, turns southeast toward Cachoeira do Sul, and then runs generally east through Rio Pardo, São Jerônimo–Triunfo and Charqueadas. The Baixo sheet labels Rio Jacuí along these successive reaches and distinguishes the Botucaraí, Pardo and southern arroio networks. This course correspondence is stronger than a nearby-name or basin-box match.

The eastern end reaches the Jacuí delta setting beside the Porto Alegre metropolitan area. The SGB report distinguishes the Jacuí, its delta and the downstream Guaíba water body. Its regional map and text support the terminal system context, but do not establish a unique local name for the model's final channel or justify replacing the entire selection with Lago Guaíba.

The separate southwestern approach travels north and then east through the Vacacaí drainage setting before joining the Jacuí upstream of Cachoeira do Sul. The SGB full-basin map and direct tributary descriptions distinguish this western branch from the Jacuí trunk. Vacacaí remains branch context; this finding does not allocate an individual official hydronym to every modeled feeder vertex.

The eastern group occupies the Taquari–Antas drainage: a long east-to-west upper approach, intermediate western bends and a southward lower approach that joins the Jacuí near the Triunfo sector. Two northern feeder corridors join that branch, rather than becoming additional Jacuí mainstem pieces. The SGB map distinguishes the Taquari–Antas drainage from the Jacuí and maps its connection. Exact Antas/Taquari naming-transition and feeder names are deliberately left unassigned at this scope.

correspondence: The complete cached route was inspected: its western upper approach descends south, turns southeast into the main southward corridor, makes the broad southern and northeastern bend, then turns southeast through the reservoir setting toward the coast.

TPWD's original statewide river map separately labels West Nueces River and the upper Nueces River. The selected western approach corresponds to the West Nueces corridor; it does not follow the map's separate upper Nueces branch. TPWD's West Nueces account identifies its downstream junction with the Nueces northwest of Uvalde.

The TSSWCB report's location and streamgage maps match the downstream Nueces sequence through Uvalde, Zavala and Dimmit counties, the broad La Salle bend and return toward McMullen and Live Oak counties. Its map distinguishes Lake Corpus Christi on this route from Choke Canyon Reservoir on the separate Frio branch.

The TPWD river map continues the same lower corridor toward the Corpus Christi coastal setting. Its waterways account places Lake Corpus Christi on the Nueces upstream of Nueces Bay. Its Region N descriptions separately identify the Nueces reaches above the reservoir, between its dam and the Calallen barrier, and from Calallen to Nueces Bay.

correspondence.finding: The selected eastern hook lies in the Mount Igikpak headwater setting, turns north and then west, and follows the upper Noatak valley toward Lake Matcharak and the Noatak National Preserve boundary. The 2014 Gates of the Arctic map depicts this continuous branch separately from the Alatna drainage to the east and the Kobuk drainage to the south. Its scale supports the upper-corridor identity without establishing that the first modeled point is the exact named source.

West of the Lake Matcharak setting the line follows the Noatak through the upper preserve, past the separate Aniuk approach and around the southward bend at the Cutler junction before returning north and west. The original preserve map and its geographical text support that succession. The nearby lake is kept distinct; the selected route is not claimed to cross Lake Matcharak merely because its label is close to the river.

The central course continues through the Anisak and Nimiuktuk junction settings, follows the broad northern bend and then the canyon corridor, and proceeds west past the Kaluktavik and Kugururok approaches. The map shows the same sequence of bends and junctions as the selected line while depicting those tributaries separately.

The western fragment continues along the Noatak below the Kugururok approach, passes the Kelly junction, turns south along the lower valley by Noatak village, and follows the lower bends past the Eli and Agashashok junction settings. The 1985 preserve sheet and the 2025 visitor-use map distinguish this lower river from its tributary valleys and the surrounding management boundaries.

The selected final point is on the lower-river approach north of the coastal outlet. The 2025 map continues the river toward the outlet and coastal water beyond this selected end. Direct NPS and Rivers.gov text identifies Kotzebue Sound as the river's receiving water, but that does not make the modeled endpoint a surveyed mouth or assign a name to every delta branch.

correspondence.scope: Uinta headwater and upper Bear corridor
correspondence.finding: The southern headwater leg and successive northward bends agree with the Uinta-to-Evanston approach on Utah DWR Figure 1. The original flow chart distinguishes West Fork, East Fork and Hayden Fork near the upper river. The selected source-end leg is retained as headwater/feeder scope; an exact fork-name transition is not assigned from these generalized maps. Farther downstream, the distinctive northward Evanston leg, Woodruff Narrows passage and westward bend toward Woodruff agree with the named Bear River corridor.

correspondence.scope: Upper valley to northern Idaho turn
correspondence.finding: The line follows the mapped river north through the Randolph–Cokeville setting, then west into Bear Lake Valley and north past Montpelier toward Soda Springs. Its northern westward turn and subsequent southward descent match the Bear River on the basin map. Bear Lake lies separately to the south of that valley reach; the selected path does not traverse Bear Lake. Official prose and the flow chart distinguish the managed inlet/outlet connection with Bear Lake from the river itself.

correspondence.scope: Gem Valley, Cache Valley and lower Bear
correspondence.finding: The southward route from the Soda/Alexander reservoir setting through Gem Valley and Oneida, its entry into Cache Valley, the Cutler approach and westward canyon exit, and the descent through the lower Bear valley correspond to the named river. The maps separately show joining Malad, Cub, Logan and Little Bear routes and irrigation canals. Those joining names are not transferred to the selected line. Reservoir and dam settings support the corridor but do not establish a uniform natural-channel feature class at every vertex.

correspondence.scope: River-mouth and Great Salt Lake continuation
correspondence.finding: After the Corinne/lower Bear setting, the selected path continues south beyond the mapped river into the Bear River Bay–Great Salt Lake setting. Its lakeward bend runs around the southern Promontory Mountains and continues northwest into the Gunnison Bay setting. The UGS overview map distinguishes Bear River, Bear River Bay, Gilbert Bay, Gunnison Bay and the railroad causeway. It depicts these lake areas as waterbody extents, not as an onward river channel named Bear River. Fragment 9767 is within this terminal-lake continuation; the tail of fragment 9766 already extends beyond the named river corridor. The model fragment join is therefore not treated as the river mouth.

Utah DWR states that Bear River ends in Great Salt Lake. UGS describes Great Salt Lake as a terminal lake and maps two different water-surface extents, while distinguishing causeways and evaporation ponds. The modeled lake crossing does not establish a present navigable or flowing channel, a current hydraulic passage through a causeway, a fixed shoreline, or an outlet from the endorheic lake. Its geometrical endpoint is not assigned the status of a natural river mouth.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
